strengths: SFTMix addresses a relevant NLP problem with a simple regularization objective that uses existing instruction-tuning data without requiring additional annotations.

Tables 1–2 report consistently positive results against matched NTP baselines across two model families, two instruction-following datasets, and medical adaptation. Overall MT-Bench gains are approximately 0.20–0.29 points; medical macro-average accuracy improves by 1.33 and 1.66 percentage points.

The evaluation combines conversational benchmarks, length-controlled preference evaluation, and medical question answering. Appendix A provides standard errors, offering useful evidence beyond selected qualitative examples.

The ablations examine the reference model, regularization strength, and use of each data subset. Comparable results using Gemma-2B confidence estimates are encouraging evidence that the reference model can be smaller than the tuned model.
weaknesses: The central claim that training dynamics are crucial is not adequately isolated. There is no same-data random-pairing Mixup baseline or comparison with confidence from a single checkpoint. Section 5.4 changes the response corpus as well as the pairing criterion, so its negative result cannot establish the necessity of confidence-guided pairing. This missing control is the principal concern preventing a clear Findings recommendation.

The proposed mechanism remains speculative. Figure 2 visualizes selected confidence extremes but does not demonstrate overfitting or improved generalization specifically on low-confidence examples. Equation 4 interpolates language-model-head outputs; smoother behavior between semantic representations does not automatically follow from this operation. Held-out subset analyses or learning curves are needed to support the claimed mechanism.

The uncertainty analysis does not establish robustness across training runs. Reported standard errors concern repeated evaluations, with no documented independent fine-tuning seeds or paired significance analysis. Some improvements are small relative to evaluation variability: Mistral on Alpaca gains about 0.32 points in length-controlled win rate, while the respective standard errors are 0.17 and 0.28. The repeated claims of significant improvement therefore exceed the demonstrated evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful optimizer and training settings. Checkpoint timing, pair sampling, maximum sequence length, implemented loss normalization, and the hyperparameter-selection protocol are insufficiently specified, and no implementation is linked. Equation 2 also computes mean negative log-likelihood rather than perplexity; averaging these quantities across checkpoints can produce different rankings, so the equation and description should be reconciled.

The broader contribution is insufficiently contextualized against alternative regularizers. NTP is the only controlled baseline, despite the discussion of NEFTune and prior cartography-based Mixup. Direct comparisons and a clearer methodological distinction from Park and Caragea (2022) would strengthen the case for main-conference publication.

Practical scalability is asserted more broadly than demonstrated. The method requires reference-model training and dataset scoring across checkpoints, but end-to-end computational overhead is not reported. Experiments on 7–8B target models and datasets spanning approximately 52K–263K examples support usefulness in those settings, rather than scalability to datasets of any size.
